# Holography {#sec-holography} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/holography.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 165–168: Gabor's invention, wavefront recording (the hologram) and wavefront reconstruction (virtual and real images).* ## Key relations A photograph records the intensity $|E|^2$ of the light scattered by an object and loses its phase, which carries the depth. Holography (Gabor, 1948, slide 165) records the phase too, by letting the object wave $U(x,y)$ interfere with a known **reference** wave $U_r(x,y)$ (slide 167). The film records $$ I(x,y)=|U_r+U|^2=|U_r|^2+|U|^2+U_r^*U+U_rU^* . $$ After development its amplitude transmittance is proportional to $I$. Illuminating it with the reference wave again (slide 168) transmits $$ U_rI=\underbrace{U_r\left(|U_r|^2+|U|^2\right)}_\text{zero order}+\underbrace{|U_r|^2\,U}_\text{object wave: virtual image} +\underbrace{U_r^2\,U^*}_\text{conjugate wave: real image}. $$ The third term is a copy of the object wave: an observer sees the object, in 3D, behind the hologram. The fourth term is the phase conjugate: it converges to a real image in front of the hologram. Recording needs **coherence**: the path difference between object and reference must stay below the coherence length (Ch. 1), and the fringes must not move by more than a fraction of their period during the exposure. This is why practical holography waited for the laser (1962, Leith and Upatnieks). Leith and Upatnieks tilted the reference by an angle $\theta$ (off-axis holography). The fringes then have period $\lambda/\sin\theta$, and the three reconstructed waves leave the hologram in different directions, so the images do not overlap. ## Record and reconstruct a hologram The panel works in one transverse dimension $x$ (a slice through a 2D hologram). Three point scatterers sit at a distance $z_0$ behind the hologram plane. The panel computes the fringe pattern $I(x)$, illuminates it with the reference and propagates the transmitted field over $0 (i - N/2)*dx); const win = x => Math.abs(x) < hg.aperture*1e-3/2 ? 1 : 0; const reRef = xs.map(x => Math.cos(k*Math.sin(th)*x)), imRef = xs.map(x => Math.sin(k*Math.sin(th)*x)); const I = xs.map((x, i) => { let re = reRef[i], im = imRef[i]; for (const [xp, a] of pts) { const r = Math.hypot(x - xp, z0), amp = hg.obj*a*Math.sqrt(z0/r)/pts.length; re += amp*Math.cos(k*r); im += amp*Math.sin(k*r); } return win(x)*(re*re + im*im); }); const re0 = xs.map((x, i) => I[i]*reRef[i]), im0 = xs.map((x, i) => -I[i]*imRef[i]); // illuminate with the conjugate reference U_r* const nz = 90, map = []; for (let j = 0; j < nz; j++) { const z = 2*z0*(j + 0.5)/nz, [R, Im] = propagate1D(re0, im0, dx, wl, z); for (let i = N/4; i < 3*N/4; i += 8) map.push({x: xs[i]*1e3, z: z*1e3, v: Math.sqrt(R[i]*R[i] + Im[i]*Im[i])}); } const fr = xs.map((x, i) => ({x: x*1e3, I: I[i]})).filter(d => Math.abs(d.x) < 0.25); return {map, fr, period: th > 0 ? wl/Math.sin(th)*1e6 : NaN, N}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 160, x: {label: "x (mm) on the hologram (central 0.5 mm)"}, y: {label: "I(x)"}, marks: [Plot.line(hgOut.fr, {x: "x", y: "I", stroke: "#0b0b0b", strokeWidth: 1})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 360, x: {label: "x (mm)"}, y: {label: "distance from the hologram z (mm)"}, color: {scheme: "magma", type: "sqrt", label: "|field|"}, marks: [Plot.dot(hgOut.map, {x: "x", y: "z", fill: "v", r: 2.2, symbol: "square"}), Plot.ruleY([hg.z0], {stroke: "#1baf7a", strokeDasharray: "4,3"})] }) ``` ```{ojs} //| echo: false html`
fringe period ${isNaN(hgOut.period) ? "(in-line: Fresnel zone pattern)" : html`λ/sin θ = ${hgOut.period.toFixed(2)} µm (${(1000/hgOut.period).toFixed(0)} lines/mm)`} · green dashed: z = z₀, where the conjugate wave focuses into the real image; the object wave diverges from the virtual image at z = −z₀ (behind the hologram)
` ``` Things to see: * The three bright foci at $z=z_0$ form the real image of the three points. Their spacing reproduces the object. * With $\theta=0$ (Gabor's in-line geometry) the real image sits on top of the zero-order beam and of the out-of-focus virtual-image wave, which blur it. Tilting the reference sends these two waves sideways, out of the image region, and the foci become clean. * Shrink the hologram: the foci broaden. The hologram is the "lens" of the imaging system and its width sets the resolution, $\approx\lambda z_0/D$ (Ch. 1, diffraction). ## Requirements on the laser ::: {#tbl-holo .cell tbl-cap='Can these sources record a hologram of a 10 cm deep scene (path difference up to 20 cm)? Coherence length ℓ_c ≈ c/(πδν) for a Lorentzian line, λ²/Δλ for a broad spectrum.' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} src = [("LED, 630 nm, Δλ = 20 nm", 630e-9, 20e-9), ("multimode FP laser diode, Δλ = 1 nm", 650e-9, 1e-9), ("multimode He–Ne (Δν ≈ 1.5 GHz)", 632.8e-9, 632.8e-9**2*1.5e9/lz.c0), ("single-mode He–Ne (Δν ≈ 1 MHz)", 632.8e-9, 632.8e-9**2*1e6/lz.c0), ("DFB / DPSS single-frequency, Δν ≈ 1 MHz", 532e-9, 532e-9**2*1e6/lz.c0)] rows = [] for name, lam, dl in src: lc = lam**2/dl rows.append({"source": name, "coherence length": f"{lc*1e3:.3g} mm" if lc < 1 else f"{lc:.3g} m", "hologram of a 10 cm deep scene?": "yes" if lc > 0.2 else "no"}) pd.DataFrame(rows) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Mechanical stability matters as much: during the exposure the fringes, with period below 1 µm, must not move by more than about $\lambda/8$. Holography tables are heavy and floated, and short pulsed lasers (Q-switched ruby, @sec-pulsed) freeze any motion, which allows holograms of people. ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **2D numerical holography.** Extend the panel to 2D with `numpy.fft.fft2`: record the hologram of a small 3D object (points at different depths) and reconstruct by propagating to several distances. This is digital holographic microscopy, where a camera replaces the film and the computer does the reconstruction. - **Computer-generated holograms.** Choose the hologram so that its diffraction pattern is a desired image (Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm). Spatial light modulators use this for optical tweezers and holographic displays. - **Volume holograms and Bragg selectivity.** A thick hologram is a 3D grating that diffracts only near the Bragg angle: the same physics as the fiber Bragg grating (Ch. 2) and the DFB laser (@sec-single-mode). It allows white-light viewing (Denisyuk holograms on banknotes) and holographic data storage. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - D. Gabor, "A new microscopic principle", *Nature* 161, 777 (1948); E. N. Leith and J. Upatnieks, *J. Opt. Soc. Am.* 52, 1123 (1962). - Kasap, sec. 4.21; Goodman, *Introduction to Fourier Optics*, 4th ed., ch. 11. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. What is the fringe period for a reference at 30° and λ = 532 nm? What film resolution (lines/mm) is needed? 2. Show from the four terms of $U_rI$ that, for an off-axis reference, the conjugate wave leaves at about $2\theta$. 3. A hologram recorded at 633 nm is reconstructed at 532 nm. Where does the real image of a point at $z_0$ appear (paraxial)? 4. Why can a hologram broken in two still show the whole object?
